newsitem.title: FRANCE: Surcharges replace by rate hikes ex-Paris/Americas.
newsitem.headline: Surcharges replace by rate hikes ex-Paris/Americas.

text.p: The scrapping of the fuel surcharge in the past few days and generally satisfactory market conditions has given several airlines scope to plan rates increases in May from France to the Americas, a Reuters survey showed
Over the past month or so, rates had increased on a number of destinations in North America ranging from five to ten centimes per kilo.

"Clearly, the dropping of the fuel surcharge has given carriers a little room for manoeuvre to increase rates but the market is responsive to this kind of move too, demand being steady on Transatlantic routes currently," an Air France cARGO official told Reuters.

Air France was planning increases of between 30 and 50 centimes/kilo on ex-Paris rates to Chicago and onward destinations in the U.S. Midwest - probably applied during the first fortnight of May, the official said.
"We increased rates by similar amounts to New York, Los Angeles and Canada last month."
The stronger dollar had meant rates increases were more readily accomodated by U.S. consignees, the official added.
American Airlines said it was raising its ex-Paris cargo rates, by between five and eight percent, effective May 5.

"We had pencilled in increases of three to five percent but we feel the market can handle more given its buoyant mood. This, coupled with the fact we wanted to make the most of an opportunity which we haven't had for some time - the last rise we applied dating back about a year or so," a Paris-based AA cargo spokesman said.

The official added: "We had a storming first quarter of 1997 and demand has been pretty strong so so far in April despite a "blip" just after Easter. French exports are faring well in the light of a stronger dollar and while there are "soft" days, overall the market is firm."
AA operates daily passenger services to New York, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and Dallas.
Meanwhile, United Airlines said it will raise its ex-Paris rates by seven and half percent, effective May 5.
UAL operates daily flights from Paris to Chicago and Washington using Boeing 777 passenger aircraft.
From July 1997, the airline will replace 767-300s on its daily service between Paris and San Francisco with 777s with cargo capacity increasing from seven to 12 tonnes per flight to 15 tonnes.
Two other belly carriers, Continental Airlines and TWA were more downbeat on current market conditions.
Continental, which operates daily routes from Paris to its Houston hub and New York/Newark, has put rates increases on hold.

"We had planned to raise rates in the Spring but a downturn in the market in recent weeks combined with the effect of price dumping by one carrier in particular, especially for freight originating in the French provinces, has knocked this idea on the head," a Paris-based cargo spokesman for the airline said.
Continental's ex-Paris volumes had been at a satisfactory level during the first quarter of 1997 but the market had gone into a bit of a slump since Easter, the official added.

Another Transatlantic carrier, TWA, echoed these comments. "We had a reasonably good first quarter but in the past couple of weeks things have gone a bit flat leaving a number of Transatlantic carriers puzzled. It's a bizarre situation because the dollar has gone from strength to strength thus improving the purchasing power of our customers. Hopefully, it's just a temporary lull."
British Airways World Cargo said it had introduced a general increase on its ex-France published rates, to destinations worldwide, effective April 1.
"The increases work out at around 13 percent on our ex-France rates for summer 1996," BA Cargo sales manager France, Roberto Casabianca, told Reuters.

BA had been accused by other carriers of dumping on its ex-France-Transatlantic rates, which had already been made even more competitive by the fact that it never applied the fuel surcharge on ex-France freight. Casabianca said France was the only European BA station which did not apply the fuel surcharge.

The allegations followed a "special offers" campaign run by the UK carrier in the first three months of 1997 on its Paris-Transatlantic routes, to promote its "known shipper security declaration," resistance to which has been strong among French forwarders but these ended with the April 1 rate increases.
BA is still running separate special offers on selected flights from the UK which began in January.
The airline had introduced the security declaration in August 1996 following the TWA aircrash only to see its freight volumes and revenues slump in the final quarter of last year, Casabianca said.

"It's true we offered very competitive rates during this campaign and probably took business away from our main European competitors such as Lufthansa, Air France and Swissair but our prices were still above those of some U.S. carriers."
Some U.S. belly carriers, he added, had offered spot rates as low as 3.50-4.00 francs /kilo to New York during the winter season compared to 5.00F/kilo for BA.

"Since April 1, our New York price is in the region of 6.50 francs/kilo and overall our rates are now within the market average and in several cases, at the top-end of the scale. They certainly reflect Air France's published rates," Casabianca said.
The begining of the summer season saw Delta Air Lines and Continental transfer their Paris' activities from Paris/Orly to Paris-Charles de Gaulle airport's Terminal 2C, alongside Air France's hub.

The French carrier has signed agreements with its two American counterparts on passenger services earlier this year, Transports Actualites, Air France Cargo chief, Francois Bachelet, said discussions would begin to consider forging an alliance on trans- Pacific freight routes.

In the LatAm zone, Air France said it was considering rates increases to Mexico City but there was little likelihood of raising prices to Sao Paulo, the French carrier already being positioned in the top bracket for rates on this buoyant route.
Varig raised its ex-Paris cargo rates by an average of eight percent, effective April 1.
The Brazilian airline operates a daily Paris-Sao Paulo-Rio passenger service.

Cargo capacity is set to rise significantly in June when Varig replaces a DC10 with an MD11 a move which will "at least double cargo lift on the route, offering between 12 and 14 tonnes per flight," a Paris-based Varig cargo official said.
In the first two months of 1997, Paris airfreight exports to Sao Paulo totalled 2,266 tonnes, up 70.9 per cent on January-February 1996, Paris airport authority figures showed.
